lessons.title: Inside a connected device: microcontrollers, flash and the boot ROM

blocks.md:
Ana buys a doorbell camera. It has a lens, a button, a Wi-Fi radio and no keyboard or screen. Ana sets it up with a phone app, and from then on it streams video to the maker's servers, which forward it to the app. Inside is a small computer that nobody will ever log in to on purpose.

An **embedded system** is a computer built into a larger product to do one job: a camera, a thermostat, a router, an insulin pump, a car's radio. **IoT** (Internet of Things) is the name for embedded devices that are connected to a network, usually the internet, and usually to a cloud service run by the maker. **Firmware** is the software built into such a device, stored in its non-volatile memory and changed only by a deliberate update.

Two kinds of hardware cover most devices:

- A **microcontroller** (MCU, microcontroller unit) is one chip holding a CPU, a small RAM, flash storage and peripherals (radios, timers, serial ports). It runs a single program, sometimes on a small **RTOS** (real-time operating system) such as FreeRTOS or Zephyr, usually with no separate user accounts or processes. Raspberry Pi's [RP2350](https://datasheets.raspberrypi.com/rp2350/rp2350-datasheet.pdf), for example, has 520 kB of on-chip SRAM and 8 kB of one-time-programmable storage, and runs code from an external flash chip of up to 16 MB.
- A **SoC** (system on chip) running **embedded Linux**: a bigger chip with a memory management unit, megabytes to gigabytes of RAM, and a full Linux kernel with a root filesystem. Routers, IP cameras and video recorders are often built this way.

The security ideas in this course apply to both; where they differ, lessons say so.

Three kinds of memory decide what can and cannot be changed later:

- **Boot ROM** (read-only memory, sometimes *mask ROM* because its contents are fixed by the masks used to make the chip): the first code the CPU runs. It cannot be changed after manufacture. CERT/CC (the CERT Coordination Center at Carnegie Mellon University, which coordinates vulnerability disclosure) says of Apple's boot ROM bug in [VU#941987](https://www.kb.cert.org/vuls/id/941987): "Because SecureROM is read-only, it cannot be patched with a firmware update."
- **OTP** (one-time programmable) memory, called **eFuses** (electronic fuses) on Espressif chips: bits that can be set once and never cleared. The RP2350 datasheet explains it uses this property for counters that can be incremented but not decremented. Keys, key fingerprints and lock flags live here.
- **Flash**: rewritable storage, often a separate chip on the board, holding the bootloader, the application and its data. Anything in flash can be updated, and anything in an external flash chip can be read by someone holding the board unless it is encrypted.

blocks.title: A connected camera: the chip, its memories and its ecosystem

scenes.caption: Inside the chip: the CPU first runs code from the boot ROM, which nobody can change after manufacture. OTP bits hold settings and key fingerprints that can be set once.
The boot ROM loads the next stage from flash. Flash is rewritable, which is what makes updates possible and what an attacker with the board in hand would like to change.
Debug pins let the factory test and program the chip. Left open, they give the same power to anyone holding the device (lesson 5).
The device is one part of a system: a phone app, the maker's cloud and an update server. A flaw in any of them can reach every device at once (lessons 9 and 13).

blocks.md: How a flash chip is divided is written down in a **partition table**. Below is a real one: the built-in "Factory app, two OTA definitions" table from Espressif's ESP-IDF (the official development framework for Espressif's ESP32 chips), as its [documentation](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/stable/esp32/api-guides/partition-tables.html) prints it. OTA means over the air: an update that arrives over the network.

blocks.code:
# ESP-IDF Partition Table
# Name, Type, SubType, Offset, Size, Flags
nvs, data, nvs, 0x9000, 0x4000,
otadata, data, ota, 0xd000, 0x2000,
phy_init, data, phy, 0xf000, 0x1000,
factory, app, factory, 0x10000, 1M,
ota_0, app, ota_0, 0x110000, 1M,
ota_1, app, ota_1, 0x210000, 1M,
blocks.caption: nvs holds settings such as Wi-Fi credentials; otadata records which app slot to boot; factory, ota_0 and ota_1 are three places an application can live. Lesson 10 uses the two OTA slots.

blocks.md:
Embedded devices differ from laptops in ways that shape every defence in this course:

- **Identical units by the thousand.** A secret or a bug in one unit is in all of them, so one discovery scales to the whole product line.
- **Unattended and headless.** No one watches a log or answers a prompt, so the device must refuse bad input and bad code on its own.
- **Long service lives and awkward updates.** That is why the UK and EU rules (lessons 4 and 14) require makers to state how long security updates will last.
- **Physically reachable.** An attacker can buy one, open it and probe the board, so the design must assume that one unit will be taken apart.

Every protection in a device rests on something that cannot change: code in boot ROM and bits in OTP. Everything in flash can be updated, by the maker or by an attacker who gets write access. Good design decides early which checks and secrets go where.

blocks.question: A researcher finds a bug in a camera. Which location of the buggy code means the maker can never fix it in units already sold?
options: The application in flash
The second-stage bootloader in flash
The boot ROM
The phone app
blocks.explain: Boot ROM is fixed when the chip is made, so its bugs stay for the life of the device (CERT/CC's note on Apple's SecureROM says exactly this). Code in flash and the phone app can be replaced by an update; a second-stage bootloader in flash is harder to update safely but still possible.

blocks.question: Why are lock flags such as 'debugging disabled' stored in OTP bits rather than in flash?
options: An OTP bit, once set, cannot be cleared by software that later gains control
OTP is faster to read at boot
Flash cannot store single bits
OTP is encrypted automatically
blocks.explain: The point of a lock is that nobody can undo it later, including malicious code. OTP bits only change one way. A flag in flash could be rewritten by anyone who can write flash. Speed and encryption are not the reason.

lessons.title: Threat modelling a device: who can reach it, and how

blocks.md:
Before choosing defences, write down what you protect and who can reach it. That is a **threat model**: a list of assets, the attackers who want them, and the paths (attack surface) by which each attacker can reach them. The US FDA's premarket cybersecurity guidance for medical devices, for example, asks makers to submit one (section V.A.1, "Threat modeling").

Tiny example, Ana's doorbell camera. Assets: live and stored video; Ana's Wi-Fi password, which the camera stores; Ana's account at the maker; the camera's ability to send traffic, which a botnet would like to borrow; and, at the maker, the firmware signing key that every camera trusts.

Then list **attacker positions**, the places from which someone can interact with the device. For embedded devices there are more than for a web app:

1. **Internet**: anyone who can send packets to a port the device exposes, or to the maker's cloud.
2. **Local network**: a compromised laptop or another device on the same Wi-Fi.
3. **Radio range**: someone within Bluetooth or Wi-Fi range during setup or use.
4. **Physical**: someone who holds a unit, opens it and connects to its debug pins or flash chip. They may own the unit, have bought one to study, or have taken one from a wall.
5. **Supply chain**: the factory, the code a vendor bought (lesson 11), and the build and signing systems.
6. **The maker's cloud and staff**: support tools that can reach every customer (lesson 13).

blocks.title: Six attacker positions around one camera

scenes.caption: Start with the device and the assets it holds: video, the Wi-Fi password, the owner's account and the device's own network access.
Remote positions first: the internet and the local network can reach whatever ports the camera leaves open. Mirai needed nothing more (lesson 3).
Proximity: during setup the camera often listens over Bluetooth Low Energy or a temporary Wi-Fi network. Anyone in range is a possible attacker.
Physical: anyone can buy one unit. If that unit gives up a secret shared by the whole fleet, the attack scales to every camera (lessons 5, 7 and 8).
Upstream: what the factory and suppliers put in, and what the maker's cloud can command. These reach every unit at once, so they carry the most weight.

blocks.md:
For each position ask the STRIDE questions (named for its six threat types: Spoofing identity, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege), and rate each threat by how many units one success affects. That last question is specific to devices: a bug that needs a screwdriver and one hour per unit is a different risk from one that works over the internet against the whole fleet, and different again from a secret extracted once by a screwdriver that then opens every unit remotely.

A threat model is most useful written as data that lives next to the code, so it is reviewed when the design changes:

blocks.code:
# threat-model.yaml (excerpt) for the doorbell camera
- id: T1
  position: internet
  threat: log in with a guessed or default password
  scale: every unit with the port open
  controls: [unique password at setup, no telnet, login rate limit]   # lesson 3
- id: T2
  position: physical
  threat: read the Wi-Fi password from the external flash chip
  scale: one unit (the owner's network)
  controls: [flash encryption with a per-device key]                  # lesson 8
- id: T3
  position: physical
  threat: extract a key shared by all units from one unit
  scale: whole fleet
  controls: [no shared secrets; per-device keys]                      # lesson 8
- id: T4
  position: supply chain
  threat: malicious firmware pushed through the update path
  scale: whole fleet
  controls: [signed images, key in a hardware security module (HSM), anti-rollback]  # lessons 6, 9
blocks.caption: A threat model as reviewable data. The scale column is the device-specific question: how many units does one success affect?

blocks.md: A common mistake is to skip the physical position because "attackers would need the device". Attackers can buy the device. The right question is what one opened unit gives them: its owner's data (acceptable for many products) or a key to all units (never acceptable).

blocks.prompt: Threat T3 needs a lab and hours of work on one unit. Threat T1 needs only a script. Which deserves more engineering effort?
blocks.reveal: Both, and T3 may be worse. T1 scales to every exposed unit cheaply. T3 is expensive once, but if the extracted secret is shared, the result also scales to every unit, remotely. The fix for T3 is design, not effort: make sure no secret on a device is worth more than that device (lesson 8).

blocks.question: Which attacker position can reach a firmware signing key that all cameras trust?
options: Someone in Bluetooth range of one camera
Someone on the owner's Wi-Fi
Someone holding one camera, if the design is correct
An intruder in the maker's build and signing systems
blocks.explain: In a correct design the signing key never leaves the maker (ideally it sits in a hardware security module); cameras hold only a fingerprint of the public key. So the supply-chain position, the maker's own build and signing systems, is the one that can reach it. Radio, LAN and physical attackers can reach only what is on a unit.

lessons.title: Default passwords: Mirai from the maker's side

blocks.md:
You met Mirai in the prerequisites: in 2016 it scanned the internet for devices answering on Telnet ports 23 and 2323 and logged in with factory defaults. The [USENIX Security 2017 study](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity17/technical-sessions/presentation/antonakakis) by Manos Antonakakis and colleagues found a list of 62 credentials, of which each bot tried 10 at random, and measured a peak of about 600,000 infected devices. This lesson looks at it from the side that could have prevented it: the manufacturer.

The authors' own conclusion: "While randomized default passwords would be a first step", devices should move "away from default-open ports to default-closed".

A **universal default password** is the same on every unit of a model, set at the factory and printed in the manual. One guess opens every unit whose owner did not change it. ETSI EN 303 645 (the European consumer IoT baseline from ETSI, the European Telecommunications Standards Institute; lesson 4) says in provision 5.1-1 that in any state other than factory default, passwords "shall be unique per device or defined by the user".

Being unique is not enough. Provision 5.1-2 requires a generation method that resists automated attacks, and the standard gives counter-examples: incremental counters ("password1", "password2"), and passwords derived from public information "such as MAC address or Wi-Fi SSID". A MAC address (media access control address, the hardware address in every network frame) is broadcast to anyone in radio range, and so is the Wi-Fi SSID (service set identifier, the network name).

blocks.code:
import hashlib, hmac, math, secrets

ALPHABET = "23456789abcdefghjkmnpqrstuvwxyz"   # 31 symbols, no 0/o/1/l/i
mac = "a4:cf:12:3b:9e:07"                     # sent in clear on every Wi-Fi frame

# 1. universal default: one guess opens every unit of the model
universal = "admin"
# 2. "unique" but derived from public data: last 3 MAC bytes
from_mac = mac.replace(":", "")[-6:]
# 3. unique and random, printed on the label at the factory
label_pw = "".join(secrets.choice(ALPHABET) for _ in range(12))

print("derived from MAC:", from_mac, "(anyone nearby can compute it)")
print("random label pw :", len(label_pw), "chars, about",
      round(12 * math.log2(len(ALPHABET))), "bits of guessing work")

# The device stores only a salted slow hash, never the password itself
salt = secrets.token_bytes(16)
stored = hashlib.scrypt(label_pw.encode(), salt=salt, n=2**14, r=8, p=1)
def check(pw):
    cand = hashlib.scrypt(pw.encode(), salt=salt, n=2**14, r=8, p=1)
    return hmac.compare_digest(cand, stored)
print("check(label_pw):", check(label_pw), " check('admin'):", check("admin"))
blocks.caption: Three provisioning schemes. Output: derived from MAC: 3b9e07 (anyone nearby can compute it) / random label pw : 12 chars, about 59 bits of guessing work / check(label_pw): True  check('admin'): False

blocks.md:
What the script shows:

- The MAC-derived password is unique per unit and still worthless: the input is public, so an attacker computes it instead of guessing it.
- A random 12-character password from a 31-symbol alphabet has $31^{12}$ possibilities, about $2^{59}$. Printed on a label inside the box, it is unique, unpredictable and usable.
- The device stores only a salted, deliberately slow hash (scrypt) and compares in constant time, so reading the flash chip does not reveal the password directly.

The other route ETSI allows is to have no factory password at all: the user must choose one during setup, before any remote access works. California's law (lesson 4) accepts the same two options.

**Rate limiting.** Provision 5.1-5 asks for a mechanism that makes brute-force guessing over the network "impracticable", for example limiting attempts per time interval with increasing delays. The script below models a login that allows 5 quick attempts, then doubles a lockout delay after each further failure, capped at one hour. It counts how many guesses an attacker gets.

blocks.code:
# Online guessing against a device that allows 5 free tries, then doubles
# a lockout delay (1 s, 2 s, 4 s ... capped at 1 hour) after each failure.
def guesses_in(seconds, free=5, cap=3600):
    t, n, delay = 0.0, 0, 1.0
    while True:
        cost = 0.1 if n < free else delay      # 100 ms per normal attempt
        if t + cost > seconds:
            return n
        t += cost; n += 1
        if n > free:
            delay = min(delay * 2, cap)
day, year = 86400, 365 * 86400
print("no limit, 1 day :", int(day / 0.1))
print("backoff, 1 day  :", guesses_in(day))
print("backoff, 1 year :", guesses_in(year))
blocks.caption: Output: no limit, 1 day : 864000 / backoff, 1 day  : 39 / backoff, 1 year : 8775

blocks.title: Online guesses an attacker gets (modelled, 100 ms per attempt)

scenes.caption: Without a limit, one attacker gets 864,000 guesses a day against one device at 100 ms per try.
With doubling delays capped at an hour, the same attacker gets 39 guesses in a day. The bar is too small to see at this scale: that is the point.
Even a full year yields only 8,775 guesses, against a 59-bit label password. Simplified: a real attacker spreads guesses over many devices, so unique passwords still matter most.

blocks.md: Lockouts can become a denial-of-service tool: an attacker can lock the real owner out by failing on purpose. ETSI notes this tension. Prefer increasing delays per source over hard account lockouts, and never lock out local recovery (a reset button that requires physical presence).

**Defender view.**
- *Prevent*: unique random credentials or user-chosen ones at setup, Telnet and other unused services off by default (ETSI 5.6-1), rate limiting.
- *Detect*: device or firewall logs showing many failed logins, inbound connections to 23 or 2323, and devices that start scanning outward. The US CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) [Mirai alert](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2016/10/14/heightened-ddos-threat-posed-mirai-and-other-botnets) also lists outbound traffic to port 48101 as a sign of infection.
- *Respond*: CISA's advice for an infected device was to disconnect, reboot (Mirai lived only in memory, so a reboot cleared it), change the password, and only then reconnect, or it could be reinfected quickly.

blocks.question: A maker sets each camera's password to the last six hex digits of its serial number, which is printed on the box and also sent in the camera's network discovery replies. Does this meet ETSI provision 5.1?
options: Yes, because the password is unique per device
No: it is derived from information an attacker can obtain, so it can be computed
Yes, if the user is told to change it
No, because passwords must be at least 16 characters
blocks.explain: Uniqueness is necessary but not sufficient. ETSI 5.1-2 requires generation that resists automated attacks and names passwords derived from public information as a counter-example. A serial number sent in discovery replies is public. ETSI sets no fixed minimum length; 'tell the user' does not fix a guessable default.

blocks.question: Mirai bots did not survive a reboot. Why was rebooting alone still a poor fix?
options: The default password was unchanged, so scanning bots could log in and reinfect it soon after
Rebooting erased the device's firmware
Mirai rewrote the boot ROM
Rebooting re-enabled UPnP
blocks.explain: CISA warned that reconnecting before changing the password could lead to quick reinfection. The vulnerability was the default credential, not the malware's persistence. Mirai lived in memory and did not touch firmware or ROM.

lessons.title: The rules catch up: SB-327, ETSI EN 303 645, UK PSTI and labels

blocks.md:
For years nothing obliged a manufacturer to avoid default passwords. That changed between 2020 and 2024, and several rules now say much the same things. This lesson covers the consumer device rules; lesson 14 covers the EU Cyber Resilience Act and lesson 15 medical devices. Until the CRA applies, wireless devices sold in the EU already face cybersecurity rules under the [Radio Equipment Directive](https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/sectors/electrical-and-electronic-engineering-industries-eei/radio-equipment-directive-red_en) (Delegated Regulation 2022/30, applied from August 2025); the CRA replaces them on 11 December 2027.

Tiny example: a company wants to sell the doorbell camera in California, the UK and the EU. Three rule sets apply, and one design, unique passwords, a published way to report bugs and a stated update period, satisfies the core of all three.

**California SB-327** (a Senate Bill that became Civil Code sections 1798.91.04 to 1798.91.06), operative 1 January 2020. [Section 1798.91.04](https://california.public.law/codes/civil_code_section_1798.91.04) requires a "reasonable security feature" for connected devices, and says that a device with a means of authentication from outside a local network meets it if either "the preprogrammed password is unique to each device manufactured" or the device "requires a user to generate a new means of authentication before access is granted to the device for the first time." [Section 1798.91.06](https://california.public.law/codes/civil_code_section_1798.91.06) states there is no private right of action: the Attorney General, city attorneys, county counsel and district attorneys enforce it. It also does not apply to devices whose functionality is already subject to security requirements under federal law, regulations or agency guidance.

**ETSI EN 303 645**, *Cyber Security for Consumer Internet of Things: Baseline Requirements* (EN means European Norm; current version [V3.1.3, 2024-09](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_en/303600_303699/303645/03.01.03_60/en_303645v030103p.pdf)). Its 13 provision groups read like a design checklist:

1. No universal default passwords
2. Implement a means to manage reports of vulnerabilities
3. Keep software updated
4. Securely store sensitive security parameters
5. Communicate securely
6. Minimize exposed attack surfaces
7. Ensure software integrity
8. Ensure that personal data is secure
9. Make systems resilient to outages
10. Examine system telemetry data
11. Make it easy for users to delete user data
12. Make installation and maintenance of devices easy
13. Validate input data

**UK PSTI** (the Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act 2022 and its 2023 Regulations) came into effect on **29 April 2024**. [GOV.UK's guidance](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-uk-product-security-and-telecommunications-infrastructure-product-security-regime) lists three requirements:

1. **Passwords** must be unique per product or defined by the user. Unique ones must not be based on incremental counters, publicly available information, or unique product identifiers such as a serial number (unless derived with an encryption method or keyed hash accepted as good industry practice), and must not be "otherwise easily guessable".
2. **How to report security issues**: the manufacturer must publish a contact and say when a reporter can expect an acknowledgement and status updates.
3. **Minimum security update period**: published, with an end date, understandable without technical knowledge.

The Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS) enforces it. These three map directly onto ETSI provisions 5.1, 5.2 and 5.3.

blocks.title: When the consumer and device rules arrived

scenes.caption: January 2020: California SB-327 becomes operative, the first US state law against shared default passwords. Axis: years from the start of 2020.
29 March 2023: the FDA's section 524B authority for 'cyber devices' takes effect (lesson 15).
29 April 2024: UK PSTI applies: unique passwords, a reporting contact and a stated update period.
EU Cyber Resilience Act: in force 10 December 2024, vulnerability reporting from 11 September 2026, fully applicable 11 December 2027 (lesson 14).

blocks.md: **Labels.** The US is building a voluntary label, the **U.S. Cyber Trust Mark**, run by the FCC (Federal Communications Commission) and likened to the Energy Star label: a mark plus a QR code leading to security information such as the maker's support period. As [Nextgov reported in October 2026](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/10/fcc-commissioner-hopes-cyber-trust-mark-products-reach-shoppers-within-year/416878/), the FCC chose the ioXt Alliance (an industry group that certifies IoT device security) as lead administrator in April 2026 after UL Solutions, a testing and certification company, withdrew following an FCC national security review, and labelled products had not yet reached shelves. Treat its details as still settling.

blocks.caption: Output: three PASS lines. A real gate would also check the published support date is visible at the point of sale.

blocks.question: A maker sells a smart plug in California whose app-based setup forces the owner to choose a password before the plug accepts any remote command. There is no factory password. Under SB-327's safe harbour, is that enough on passwords?
options: No, the password must also be printed on the box
No, SB-327 requires two-factor authentication
Yes: requiring the user to set a new means of authentication before first access is one of the two listed options
Only if the plug has no local network interface
blocks.explain: Section 1798.91.04(b) lists two ways to meet the reasonable-security test for remote authentication: a unique preprogrammed password, or a feature requiring the user to generate a new means of authentication before first access. The plug uses the second. Neither MFA nor printed passwords are required by the statute.

blocks.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three UK PSTI requirements?
options: Unique or user-defined passwords
Mandatory third-party penetration testing
Published information on how to report security issues
A published minimum period of security updates
blocks.explain: GOV.UK's guidance lists passwords, how to report security issues, and the minimum security update period. PSTI does not require third-party testing; it requires a statement of compliance to accompany the product.

lessons.title: Debug ports: UART, JTAG and SWD, and how makers lock them

blocks.md:
Open almost any device and you find small unlabelled pads or pin headers. Many are **debug interfaces**: the doors the factory uses to program the chip, test the board and diagnose faults. They are useful for exactly the reason they are dangerous: they give whoever is connected deep control of the chip.

Tiny example: during development, the doorbell camera prints its boot log on a serial port and offers a shell prompt there. If that prompt ships in the product, anyone who opens the case and attaches a cheap USB-to-serial adapter gets a shell, usually as root.

The three you will meet most:

- **UART** (universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter): a simple two-wire serial port (transmit and receive) that carries text, such as a boot log or a console. "Asynchronous" because no shared clock wire is used.
- **JTAG**: named after the Joint Test Action Group, a group of European and North American companies that formed in 1985 to solve the problem of testing crowded circuit boards, as a [Texas Instruments paper](https://www.ti.com/lit/an/scta028/scta028.pdf) recounts. Their work became the standard IEEE 1149.1, *Test Access Port and Boundary-Scan Architecture*. Chips reuse the same port for debugging: halting the CPU, reading and writing memory and registers, and programming flash.
- **SWD** (Serial Wire Debug): Arm's two-pin alternative, a clock (SWCLK) and one bidirectional data pin (SWDIO), which, as [SEGGER's reference](https://kb.segger.com/SWD) puts it, provides "all the normal JTAG debug and test functionality".

Why makers leave them: the factory needs them to program and test each unit, and repair centres need them for returned devices. Why it matters: a working debug port gives the holder the same power as the factory, and if the chip's protections allow it, can read out firmware and any secrets stored with it.

ETSI EN 303 645 addresses this directly:

- Provision 5.6-4A: "Debug interfaces shall be disabled or protected via a best practice authentication or access control mechanism." Its example: a UART "is disabled through the bootloader software", with "no logon prompt and no interactive menu".
- Provision 5.6-4B: debug ports should be physically protected, for example by a case that cannot be opened without tools or breaking it.
- Provision 5.6-3: hardware should not unnecessarily expose physical interfaces, for example a micro-USB port meant only for power should not also allow debug commands.

How chips lock debug, from two vendors' documentation:

- **Espressif ESP32**: the [ESP-IDF security guide](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/stable/esp32/security/security.html) says the JTAG interface "stays disabled if any of the security features are enabled" (secure boot or flash encryption), and can also be disabled by an eFuse on its own. The ROM's UART download mode, used to flash the chip over serial, stays disabled in release configurations or can be disabled at runtime.
- **Raspberry Pi RP2350**: the [datasheet](https://datasheets.raspberrypi.com/rp2350/rp2350-datasheet.pdf) offers OTP flags DEBUG_DISABLE and SECURE_DEBUG_DISABLE, or a 128-bit **debug key** installed in OTP that keeps debug locked until the key is presented: an authenticated way back in for repair, instead of all or nothing.

The OTP bits are one-way, so no software can clear them. On the RP2350, though, Secure software can re-enable debug through the DEBUGEN register unless DEBUGEN_LOCK is set, so set that lock as well.

blocks.title: One chip through its life: open, locked, and service mode

scenes.caption: On the line the port is open: the factory station programs flash and runs board tests over JTAG or SWD.
Danger: if the unit ships like this, anyone who opens the case can do what the factory did, including reading the firmware out.
The last factory step burns an OTP lock. The debug logic refuses connections, and no later software can clear the bit.
Authenticated debug: on chips that support it, a repair centre presents a per-device key and gets access; everyone else still sees a locked port.

blocks.md: The UART console is software, so it is locked in the bootloader or application. Below, a toy bootloader decides what the serial port offers. Engineering builds get a shell; production builds get a read-only boot log unless the debug fuse is unburned or a signed, per-device unlock token is presented.

blocks.caption: Production build output: uart: boot log, no input. Built with -DDEV_BUILD it prints uart: root shell, which is why release builds must never be compiled with that flag.

blocks.md: Do not rely on hiding the pads (no labels, pins removed, epoxy). Those slow a curious owner and stop nobody determined. Treat physical obscurity as a delay, and make the chip itself refuse: burned debug fuses, disabled ROM download modes, no console login.

**Defender view.** Before release, check on a production unit (your own) that the console gives no prompt, that the debug port refuses a connection, and that the ROM's serial download mode is off; record the fuse state in the factory log for every unit. Locked debug is necessary but not sufficient: lesson 7 shows how physical attackers try to get around it, and why no unit should hold secrets that matter beyond itself. Reading firmware images you are authorised to analyse is covered in *Binary reverse engineering in depth* (lessons "Firmware images" and "Inside extracted firmware").

blocks.question: A camera's release firmware prints its boot log on UART and stops at a login prompt protected by a password that is the same on every unit. Does it meet ETSI 5.6-4A?
options: Yes, because the interface is protected by a password
Yes, because UART is not a debug interface
No, because boot logs must never be printed
No: a universal password is not a best-practice access control, and ETSI's example is no prompt at all
blocks.explain: 5.6-4A requires debug interfaces to be disabled or protected by best-practice authentication. A password shared by every unit fails that and also breaks provision 5.1. A read-only boot log is not forbidden by itself; the interactive login is the problem.

blocks.question: Why does an RP2350 debug key (rather than a plain DEBUG_DISABLE fuse) suit a medical device maker that repairs returned units?
options: It keeps debug locked for everyone except a holder of the key, so authorised repair is still possible
It makes the debug port faster
It lets the owner reset the fuse
It encrypts the firmware
blocks.explain: A plain disable flag is permanent for everyone, including the maker. A debug key installed in OTP keeps debug locked until the key is presented, giving an authenticated service path. It does not change speed, fuses cannot be reset, and encryption is a separate feature.

lessons.title: Secure boot: a chain of trust that starts in ROM

blocks.md:
A **digital signature** is a value computed over data with a private key that only its owner holds; anyone with the matching public key can check it, and any change to the data makes the check fail. **Secure boot** means a device runs only code its maker signed. Each stage checks the signature of the next before running it, so trust passes link by link from code nobody can change. That sequence is the **chain of trust**, and its first link is the **root of trust**: the boot ROM plus a key fingerprint in OTP.

Tiny example: an attacker on the camera's network finds a way to write flash. Without secure boot, they write their own firmware and it runs on every boot, invisibly and permanently. With secure boot, the modified image fails its check and the camera refuses to run it.

What a real chip does. Espressif's [Secure Boot v2 documentation](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/stable/esp32/security/secure-boot-v2.html) for the ESP32:

1. The ROM checks a secure boot bit in eFuse. If set, it verifies the second-stage bootloader's RSA-PSS signature (RSA is a widely used public-key algorithm; RSA-PSS is an RSA signature scheme with a probabilistic padding, PSS meaning probabilistic signature scheme), "If this fails, the boot process will be aborted."
2. The bootloader then verifies the application image the same way.
3. The public key travels inside each image's signature block; only "a digest of the RSA-3072 public key is stored in the eFuse". The ROM compares the image's key against that digest first.

The RP2350 does the same with ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) on the secp256k1 curve, a standard elliptic curve: hash the image with SHA-256, verify the signature with the public key carried in the image, and check that key's SHA-256 fingerprint against OTP.

blocks.title: The chain of trust, link by link

nodes.label:
OTP: SHA-256 of
maker's public key

scenes.caption: The root of trust: ROM code that cannot change and a key fingerprint in OTP that cannot change. Everything else is judged against these two.
The ROM verifies the bootloader's signature and that the signing key matches the fingerprint. Only then does it jump to it.
The bootloader repeats the check for the application. A failure at any link stops the boot, so trust is never extended to unverified code.
The private key never touches a device. It lives at the maker, ideally in a hardware security module (HSM). Its leak would break every link at once.

blocks.md: The script below builds a toy version so you can see each check fire. Our firmware image is the code bytes, then the 32-byte public key, then a 64-byte signature. We use Ed25519 signatures (a modern elliptic-curve signature scheme with 32-byte keys and 64-byte signatures) for brevity; the ESP32 uses RSA-PSS and the RP2350 ECDSA, but the logic is the same. It runs three images: a good one, the good one with one bit flipped, and one properly signed by a different key.

blocks.code:
import hashlib
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ed25519 import (
    Ed25519PrivateKey, Ed25519PublicKey)
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.serialization import Encoding, PublicFormat
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidSignature

def raw(pub): return pub.public_bytes(Encoding.Raw, PublicFormat.Raw)

vendor = Ed25519PrivateKey.from_private_bytes(bytes(range(32)))  # toy key
OTP_FINGERPRINT = hashlib.sha256(raw(vendor.public_key())).digest()

def sign(fw, key):        # build server: image = code + public key + signature
    return fw + raw(key.public_key()) + key.sign(fw)

def rom_boot(image):      # boot ROM: fixed code, trusts only the fingerprint
    fw, pub, sig = image[:-96], image[-96:-64], image[-64:]
    if hashlib.sha256(pub).digest() != OTP_FINGERPRINT:
        return "REFUSE: key not ours"
    try:
        Ed25519PublicKey.from_public_bytes(pub).verify(sig, fw)
    except InvalidSignature:
        return "REFUSE: bad signature"
    return "BOOT " + fw.decode()

good = sign(b"camera-fw v1.4", vendor)
print(rom_boot(good))
bad = bytearray(good); bad[0] ^= 0x01           # flip one bit of the code
print(rom_boot(bytes(bad)))
attacker = Ed25519PrivateKey.from_private_bytes(bytes(32))
print(rom_boot(sign(b"evil-fw v9.9", attacker)))  # signed, but by the wrong key
print("OTP fingerprint", OTP_FINGERPRINT.hex()[:16], "...")
blocks.caption: Output: BOOT camera-fw v1.4 / REFUSE: bad signature / REFUSE: key not ours / OTP fingerprint 56475aa75463474c ...

blocks.title: Tracing rom_boot on the three images

scenes.caption: Good image: split into code, key and signature.
The key's hash matches the OTP fingerprint, so the ROM accepts this key as the maker's.
The signature verifies over the code, so the image boots.
Tampered image: one bit of the code flipped. The key still matches, but the signature no longer covers these bytes.
Attacker's image: a valid signature, made with the attacker's own key. The fingerprint check stops it before signature checking matters.

blocks.md: Two classic mistakes. First, checking a hash without a signature: a hash (or CRC) catches corruption but anyone can recompute it for their own image. Second, trusting the public key inside the image without comparing it to the fingerprint in OTP: then any key the attacker generates is "valid". The fingerprint check is what binds the image to the maker.

**When the root itself is flawed.** In 2019 a researcher known as axi0mX published checkm8, an exploit for a use-after-free bug in the boot ROM ("SecureROM") of Apple chips A5 to A11. CERT/CC's [VU#941987](https://www.kb.cert.org/vuls/id/941987) explains why it mattered: the ROM "cannot be patched with a firmware update", so the only fix that guarantees immunity is new hardware. It also records the limits: it needs physical access with the device in DFU (Device Firmware Update) mode, it does not persist across reboot, and data protected by the Secure Enclave stays protected without the passcode. Lesson: keep the ROM small and simple, because its bugs are forever, and design so that a ROM bypass on one unit does not unlock others.

**Key choices last as long as the silicon.** The algorithm and key fingerprint in OTP stay for the device's life. NIST IR 8547 ([final, October 2026](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/ir/8547/final)) deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve signatures after 2030 and disallows them after 2035, because a large quantum computer could forge them. For a device designed now, plan for post-quantum signatures: NIST standardised the stateful hash-based schemes LMS and XMSS in [SP 800-208](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/208/final) (2020) and the lattice-based ML-DSA in [FIPS 204](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/204/final) (2024), and some chips let you register several key slots so a key can later be revoked (the RP2350 has KEY_INVALID bits for this).

blocks.question: A bootloader computes SHA-256 of the application and compares it with a hash stored next to the application in flash. What does this protect against?
options: An attacker who can write flash replacing the application
Accidental corruption of the application, but not deliberate replacement
Both corruption and replacement
Neither
blocks.explain: Whoever can write the new application can also write its new hash, so a bare hash only detects accidents. A signature checked against a key fingerprint the attacker cannot change (in OTP) is what stops deliberate replacement.

blocks.question: Why does the ROM compare the hash of the image's public key with OTP, instead of storing the whole public key in OTP?
options: Hashes are more secure than keys
The ROM cannot read OTP
OTP space is small: a 32-byte fingerprint pins a much larger key (an RSA-3072 key is hundreds of bytes)
So that anyone can change the key later
blocks.explain: OTP is tiny (8 kB on the RP2350) and costly per bit. A SHA-256 fingerprint fixes exactly one key, as securely as storing it, in 32 bytes. ESP32 stores the digest of its RSA-3072 key the same way. It does not make the key changeable; that is the point of OTP.

lessons.title: Hands on the chip: fault injection, and code that resists it

blocks.md:
Locked debug and secure boot assume the chip executes its instructions correctly. A physical attacker can try to make it misbehave on purpose: **fault injection** disturbs a chip for a moment so that an instruction is skipped or a value is read wrongly. A **glitch** is the brief disturbance itself: a dip in the supply voltage, a distorted clock, an electromagnetic pulse, or a focused laser pulse.

Tiny example: boot code computes "signature valid?" and then branches on the answer. If one disturbance makes the CPU skip the branch at the right moment, a bad image boots. This lesson explains the mechanism at the design level and shows how code and hardware are hardened; it does not teach how to glitch any product.

**A real, public test.** In 2024 Raspberry Pi offered a prize to anyone who could read a secret from the OTP of a locked RP2350. Several attacks succeeded, and Raspberry Pi recorded each one as an **erratum** (a documented flaw in a chip, with its workaround if there is one) in appendix D of the [RP2350 datasheet](https://datasheets.raspberrypi.com/rp2350/rp2350-datasheet.pdf).

The RP2350 also has **glitch detectors**: circuits that notice a disturbed clock or core supply voltage and reset the chip rather than let software run on in an undefined state. They are off by default and are armed by an OTP flag.

Four findings, each credited in the datasheet errata:

- **E16** (Aedan Cullen): disturbing the OTP memory's supply voltage while security settings were read at reset could make a guarded read pass with the wrong data, enabling debug and undoing the secure boot and debug-disable flags.
- **E20** (Marius Muench): a precisely timed glitch during a legitimate call to the boot ROM's reboot function could send it down a path that later runs attacker-chosen code as Secure.
- **E21** (Thomas Roth): two precisely timed glitches on entry to the USB bootloader could leave a page of OTP unlocked.
- **E24** (Kévin Courdesses): swapping the flash contents at the right moment, combined with a glitch, made the boot ROM check the signature of different data from the code it then ran. Its workaround reads "None"; only a new chip revision (A4) fixed it.

All four need the chip in hand, special equipment and precise timing. None scales over a network.

Three lessons for designers follow from those errata:

1. **Physical attacks on one unit are a matter of effort and equipment, not of possibility.** Plan as if a determined lab can get one unit's secrets out.
2. **Every unused path is attack surface**: boot modes, bootloader commands and reboot types you do not need should be turned off in OTP (RP2350 offers flags to disable the USB bootloader interfaces and reboots to a chosen code address).
3. **Code can raise the cost**: redundant checks, values that are hard to produce by accident, and a default of "refuse".

MCUboot (an open-source secure bootloader for microcontrollers) ships a "Fault Injection Hardening" option, and its [design notes](https://docs.mcuboot.com/design.html) describe testing it by scripted instruction skips in an emulator.

Our own simulator below models boot code as a list of steps and tries skipping each single step on a bad image. The naive version has two flaws: its flag starts as "ok" and it checks once. The hardened version starts from "refuse", verifies twice into unlikely constants (0x3CA5965A instead of 1, so a corrupted or skipped write cannot accidentally produce it) and rechecks before booting.

blocks.caption: Output: naive   : 3 steps, single skips that boot a bad image: [0, 1] / hardened: 5 steps, single skips that boot a bad image: []

blocks.title: Which single skipped step lets a bad image boot?

scenes.caption: Each cell is one step. The image being booted is bad, so every correct run must end in a halt.
Naive, skip step 0: verify never runs, the flag keeps its initial value 'ok', and the bad image boots. The flaw is a default of allow.
Naive, skip step 1: the halt decision is never made, so the boot step runs. One branch was the only guard.
Hardened: skipping any one of the five steps still ends in a halt, because two results must both equal the unlikely constant and boot rechecks them.

blocks.md: Hardening raises cost; it does not make a chip invulnerable. The RP2350 errata show two glitches defeating an OTP lock-down (E21) and a glitch that changed which data was signature-checked (E24), both on a chip designed with fault attacks in mind. That is why lesson 8 insists that no unit holds a secret whose loss affects other units.

**Defender view.** Choose chips with documented fault countermeasures and published errata, enable glitch detectors and turn off unused boot paths during provisioning, use the bootloader's hardening options, and keep fleet-wide secrets off the device. For devices in public places, add tamper detection (case switches, enclosures) that wipes keys. Read vendor errata as part of vulnerability management, as you would CVEs.

blocks.question: In the naive simulator, why does skipping the very first step let a bad image boot?
options: Because the result flag was initialised to 'ok', so never computing it left it saying ok
Because verify() returns True for bad images
Because the CPU jumps to the application directly
Because the image is signed
blocks.explain: verify() would have returned False, but it never ran. The flag kept its initial value, which was 'ok'. Initialising security decisions to 'refuse' (default deny) removes that path.

blocks.question: Raspberry Pi's mitigation for the reboot-path attack was an OTP flag that disables rebooting to a chosen code address when the application does not need it. What general principle is this?
options: Security through obscurity
Defence by encryption
Rate limiting
Reduce attack surface: turn off features you do not use
blocks.explain: The attack used a reboot feature most products never need. Disabling it removes the path entirely, the same principle as turning off Telnet or unused interfaces (ETSI 5.6). Nothing was hidden, encrypted or rate limited.

lessons.title: Device secrets: per-device keys, secure elements and House of Keys

blocks.md:
A device holds secrets: the owner's Wi-Fi password, a key to authenticate to the maker's cloud, perhaps keys to decrypt stored video. The design question from lesson 2 is: what does one opened unit give an attacker? The answer should be "that unit's secrets", never "every unit's".

Tiny example: if every camera of a model authenticates to the cloud with the same API key baked into firmware, then reading one flash chip, or one public firmware download, lets an attacker pose as any camera.

**Case: House of Keys (2015).** Stefan Viehböck of the security consultancy SEC Consult [analysed firmware images](https://sec-consult.com/blog/detail/house-of-keys-industry-wide-https) for more than 4,000 embedded devices from over 70 vendors and found more than 580 unique private keys for HTTPS certificates and SSH host keys, shared across units and sometimes across vendors. Matching them against internet scans showed at least 230 in active use: keys for more than 9 percent of HTTPS hosts on the web (3.2 million hosts) and more than 6 percent of SSH hosts. CERT/CC's [VU#566724](https://www.kb.cert.org/vuls/id/566724) explains the consequence, impersonation, man-in-the-middle and passive decryption, and the root cause: common SDKs (software development kits) and ISP-provided firmware. Nine months later SEC Consult reported that the number of devices using known HTTPS keys had grown by 40 percent (3.2 million to 4.5 million).

ETSI EN 303 645 turns this into rules:

- 5.4-3: hard-coded critical security parameters in software source code "shall not be used", and the standard warns that simple obfuscation "can be trivially broken".
- 5.4-4: keys used to protect communication with the maker's services "shall be unique per device".
- 5.4-1: secrets in persistent storage shall be stored securely; it names a TEE (trusted execution environment, an isolated mode of the main processor), a secure element and hardware-backed encrypted storage.

Note what ETSI says does *not* need to be unique: the maker's public key used to verify updates (lessons 6 and 9). Public keys are not secrets.

scenes.caption: Shared design: every unit carries the same key and the cloud accepts it. It works fine until anyone reads it out of one unit or one firmware file.
One opened unit yields the key, and the attacker can now pose as any camera, or decrypt traffic of all of them. The whole fleet fails together.
Per-device design: each unit has its own key, generated inside a secure element. The cloud keeps only public keys, so one extracted key is one revoked unit.

labels.k:
Own key per unit
(in secure element)

blocks.md:
Where per-device secrets live, from weakest to strongest:

- **Plain flash**: readable by anyone with the chip. Never for anything that matters.
- **Encrypted flash**: on the ESP32, [flash encryption](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/stable/esp32/security/flash-encryption.html) encrypts the off-chip flash with an AES (Advanced Encryption Standard, the standard symmetric cipher) key held in eFuses that software cannot read, so "physical readout of flash will not be sufficient to recover most flash contents". Espressif recommends a unique key per device and release mode, which stops the ROM serial loader from decrypting.

Stronger places for per-device secrets:

- **TEE**: Arm TrustZone splits a chip into a secure and a non-secure world; [Trusted Firmware-M](https://trustedfirmware-m.readthedocs.io/en/latest/introduction/readme.html) is a reference secure-world firmware for Cortex-M chips.
- **Secure element**: a separate tamper-resistant chip that generates a key inside, never exports it, and only performs operations with it (sign this, decrypt that).

AWS's IoT documentation recommends [a unique certificate per device](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/iot/latest/developerguide/x509-client-certs.html), noting that private keys can be burned into secure storage so that "sensitive cryptographic material never leaves the device".

blocks.caption: A toy secure element and challenge-response login. Output: cam-0001 as itself  : accepted / cam-0002 posing as 1: rejected / revoke cam-0001 only: True | fleet still trusted: ['cam-0000', 'cam-0002']

blocks.md: The toy shows three properties of per-device identity. The cloud sends a fresh random challenge each time, so a recorded answer is useless later. A device cannot pose as another, because it holds only its own key. And a compromised unit is revoked alone by deleting one registry entry, while the rest of the fleet keeps working. Python's double-underscore attribute is only a stand-in for "no export function"; real protection comes from hardware.

Design rule: the worst outcome of fully compromising one unit should be the loss of that unit. Achieve it with per-device keys generated on the device, public keys in the cloud, and no shared secrets in firmware.

blocks.question: Which of these does ETSI EN 303 645 say need NOT be unique per device?
options: The key a device uses to authenticate to the maker's cloud
A pre-installed login password
The maker's public key used to verify update signatures
The key protecting stored Wi-Fi credentials
blocks.explain: A public key is not secret, so sharing it across devices leaks nothing; ETSI's example 6 under provision 5.4-4 says so. Cloud authentication keys and passwords must be unique (5.4-4, 5.1-1), and stored secrets must be protected (5.4-1).

blocks.question: House of Keys traced some shared keys to chipset vendors' SDKs that many device makers built on. Who is best placed to fix this for future devices?
options: Each device owner, by rotating keys manually
The SDK and firmware makers, by generating a unique key on each device at first boot or in the factory
Browser vendors, by blocking the certificate
ISPs, by filtering HTTPS
blocks.explain: CERT/CC notes owners can sometimes replace keys but often cannot. The root cause is a key baked into shared firmware, so the fix belongs upstream: generate a key per unit. Blocking a certificate or filtering traffic treats symptoms and breaks legitimate use.

lessons.title: Signed updates and anti-rollback: what a device must check

blocks.md:
A device that cannot be updated keeps every bug it shipped with. A device that accepts any update can be given anyone's firmware. Secure updating sits between: the device accepts new firmware only from its maker, only for itself, and never older than what it already trusts.

Tiny example: version 1.1 of the camera firmware has a remote bug, fixed in 2.0. An attacker who cannot sign firmware takes the genuine, correctly signed 1.1 image from the maker's website and offers it to cameras as an "update". Every signature check passes. Only a version rule stops this **downgrade** (or **rollback**) attack.

ETSI EN 303 645 provision 5.3-10 says that where updates arrive over a network, the device "shall verify the authenticity and integrity of each update via a trust relationship", and lists a digital signature as one valid trust relationship. A TLS connection to the update server is another, but it only protects the download: it does not prove who built the image, it fails if the server itself is compromised, and it does nothing for updates arriving by USB stick. Signing the image itself protects it wherever it travels.

The IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) working group SUIT (Software Updates for Internet of Things) wrote the questions an update must answer into [RFC 9019](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9019.html) (April 2021), and answers them with a signed **manifest**: a small metadata document that travels with the image.

blocks.title: RFC 9019: what the manifest lets the device check

nodes.label:
Meant for me?
(vendor, class, device id)

scenes.caption: The image alone says nothing about itself. The manifest carries the facts the device needs, and is signed so they cannot be altered.
First: is the signer one of my trust anchors? Second: does the image's digest match the one in the manifest? Together these give authenticity and integrity.
Third: is it for this device? Conditions on vendor, class and device identifiers stop a valid image for another model being installed here.
Fourth: is it older than what I run? RFC 9019 notes that a device presented with an old but valid manifest must reject it; a sequence number makes that check possible.

blocks.md:
**Anti-rollback** means the device refuses images older than a floor it remembers, even when they are correctly signed. The floor must be stored somewhere an attacker cannot lower it. Two real implementations:

- **MCUboot** compares each image's *security counter* (a field inside the signed area) with a value kept in "a non-volatile and trusted component of the device", per its [design document](https://docs.mcuboot.com/design.html). The counter is separate from the version number, so ordinary releases need not bump it, and a downgrade to an image with the same counter remains possible.
- **RP2350** stores the minimum rollback version in OTP as a **thermometer code**: a unary number whose value is one plus the index of the highest set bit. OTP bits can only be set, so the counter "allows OTP rows containing counters to be incremented" but "does not allow them to be decremented". Booting a newer image burns the next bit.

blocks.caption: A thermometer counter in fuses. Output: fw 1.0 (rb 1): BOOT, fuses now 10000000 / fw 1.1 (rb 1): BOOT, fuses now 10000000 / fw 2.0 (rb 2, fixes CVE): BOOT, fuses now 11000000 / fw 1.1 (rb 1, old, signed): REFUSE (rollback 1 < floor 2)

blocks.title: The rollback floor in eight fuse bits

scenes.caption: A new chip: no bits burned, floor 0.
Firmware 1.0 carries rollback version 1. Booting it burns bit 0: floor 1. Firmware 1.1 keeps rollback version 1, so nothing changes.
Firmware 2.0 fixes a security bug and carries rollback version 2. Booting it burns bit 1: floor 2. No software can unburn it.
The attacker offers genuine, signed 1.1 (rollback 1). Signature fine, version 1 below floor 2: refused. Eight bits allow eight such security bumps over the life of the chip.

blocks.md: Fuses are a scarce, permanent budget. Bump the rollback version only when an old image has a security bug worth blocking, as MCUboot's separate security counter allows. Burn the bit only after the new image has proved it works (lesson 10), or a bad update could leave the device unable to boot anything.

**Defender view.** Sign every image with a key kept in an HSM, with two people needed to sign a release; verify on the device, not only on the server; carry a version and a rollback counter inside the signed data; and log update attempts, including refused ones, to the cloud. A spike of refused updates across a fleet is worth investigating. ETSI 5.3-13 and UK PSTI also require you to publish how long updates will come.

blocks.question: An attacker who controls the camera's network serves the genuine, signed firmware 1.1 as an update. The camera checks the signature and the device class but has no version floor. What happens?
options: It installs 1.1, bringing back the bug fixed in 2.0
It refuses, because the signature is from last year
It refuses, because TLS detects the attacker
It installs it but the bug cannot be reached
blocks.explain: Nothing in a signature says 'too old'. Without a sequence number or rollback counter checked against a stored floor, a validly signed old image is accepted, reopening fixed bugs. TLS would not help if the attacker offers the file another way or controls the server path.

blocks.question: Why does MCUboot keep a security counter separate from the version number?
options: Version numbers cannot be signed
Because the counter is encrypted
So that only security-relevant releases raise the floor, saving permanent counter space and still allowing downgrades between equally safe releases
So the counter can be decreased
blocks.explain: Its design notes say the counter need not increase with each release, and that an older image with the same counter value is still accepted. Counters in fuses are a scarce one-way budget, so raising them only for security fixes makes sense. They can never decrease.

lessons.title: A/B slots, trial boots and recovery from a bad update

blocks.md:
Updating a device in the field is risky in a way updating a laptop is not: power can fail halfway, the new image can crash on some hardware revision, and nobody is there to fix it. A device that bricks (becomes unusable) after an update becomes a recall. Worse, a fragile update path makes makers reluctant to ship security fixes at all.

Tiny example: 50,000 thermostats download version 3.2. One in a hundred has a sensor variant that makes 3.2 crash at start-up. Without a fallback, 500 homes lose heating until a technician visits.

The standard answer is **A/B** (dual-slot) updating. Flash holds two application slots; the device runs from one while the new image is written to the other, so a failed download changes nothing. ESP-IDF requires "at least two OTA app slot partitions (i.e., ota_0 and ota_1) and an OTA Data Partition", and writes the new image "to whichever OTA app slot that is currently not selected for booting", per its [OTA documentation](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/stable/esp32/api-reference/system/ota.html). The small otadata partition from lesson 1 records which slot to boot.

The second idea is the **trial boot**. The new image boots once in a pending state and must prove itself (self-test, reach the cloud) before it is marked good. If it crashes or the power fails first, the bootloader goes back to the old slot.

blocks.title: An A/B update with a trial boot (ESP-IDF states)

scenes.caption: Running 3.1 from ota_0. The download of 3.2 goes to the idle slot ota_1; if it fails midway, the device is unaffected.
Reboot into 3.2. The bootloader marks it PENDING_VERIFY: on trial.
Good path: diagnostics pass, the app calls esp_ota_mark_app_valid_cancel_rollback() and 3.2 becomes VALID. Only now is it safe to raise the anti-rollback floor.
Bad path: 3.2 crashes before confirming. On the next boot the bootloader marks it ABORTED and boots 3.1 again. The thermostat keeps heating.

blocks.md: The application's part, adapted from Espressif's example: on its first boot it checks whether it is on trial, runs its own diagnostics, and either confirms itself or asks to be rolled back. Espressif adds that if the application cannot even reach this code, "due to an abort/reboot/power loss error", the bootloader rolls back on the next boot anyway.

blocks.title: First boot of a new image (ESP-IDF API)

scenes.caption: Which slot am I running from, and what is its state?
It is on trial, because this is the first boot after the update.
Self-test. Our diagnostic also checks that the update server can be reached, so a build that cannot fetch the next fix is never confirmed.
Pass: confirm. The image is VALID and will boot normally from now on.
Fail instead: mark invalid and reboot. The bootloader picks the previous slot.

blocks.md: MCUboot offers the same ideas under different names: an update is first swapped in as a **test** swap, and "Unless the swap is made permanent, revert back on the next boot". Its swap algorithms exchange the two slots sector by sector with progress recorded in flash, so a power cut mid-swap can resume. Flash wear limits how often this can happen: MCUboot's design notes estimate that a 4 KB scratch area with 10,000 erase cycles supports about 267 upgrades of a 150 KB image.

Two different things are both called rollback. **App rollback** (this lesson) is a safety feature: go back to the last image that worked. **Anti-rollback** (lesson 9) is a security feature: never go back below a floor. They interact: ESP-IDF updates its eFuse security version only after the new app is marked valid, so a bad update can still fall back to the previous good one.

Updating a device that keeps someone alive is the extreme case. When Abbott (formerly St. Jude Medical) released a pacemaker firmware fix in 2017, CISA's [advisory ICSMA-17-241-01](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-medical-advisories/icsma-17-241-01) repeated the maker's warning that "firmware updates can cause devices to malfunction", listing "reloading of the previous firmware due to a failed upgrade" among the risks, and advised updating pacing-dependent patients where temporary pacing was available. Lesson 15 returns to this case.

blocks.question: A camera is on trial with firmware 4.0 (PENDING_VERIFY) when the power fails. What does ESP-IDF's bootloader do on the next start, with rollback enabled?
options: Boots 4.0 again and waits for confirmation
Erases both slots
Boots the factory image and burns the anti-rollback fuse
Marks 4.0 ABORTED and boots the previous valid image
blocks.explain: An image that reboots while still PENDING_VERIFY was never confirmed. ESP-IDF marks it aborted and returns to the last valid application. Nothing is erased, and the security version is only raised after a successful confirmation.

blocks.question: Why should the anti-rollback floor be raised only after the new image confirms itself?
options: Because fuses are slow to write
Because if the new image is faulty, the device must still be allowed to boot the previous image, which a raised floor would forbid
Because the floor is stored in the image
It should be raised before downloading
blocks.explain: If the floor rose at download time and the new image crashed, the only working image would now be below the floor: the device would brick. Raising it after confirmation keeps the safety fallback and the security floor compatible.

lessons.title: Ripple20: one TCP/IP stack inside hundreds of products

blocks.md:
Embedded makers rarely write their own TCP/IP stack (the code that parses IP, TCP, UDP, DNS and DHCP packets). They license one, compile it in, and often stop tracking it. When that stack has a bug, every product built on it shares the bug, and many makers do not know they ship it.

Tiny example: a printer, an infusion pump and a factory controller from three different companies all answer pings using the same licensed library. One malformed packet affects all three.

**Case: Ripple20 (June 2020).** Moshe Kol and Shlomi Oberman of JSOF, a security research firm, reported 19 vulnerabilities in the Treck TCP/IP stack, an embedded network stack, to CERT/CC. CISA's advisory [ICSA-20-168-01](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-20-168-01) lists them as CVE-2020-11896 to CVE-2020-11914. Four were rated critical:

- CVE-2020-11896 (CVSS 10.0): improper handling of a length parameter inconsistency in the IPv4/UDP component, which "may result in remote code execution".
- CVE-2020-11897 (10.0): the same bug class in IPv6, a possible out-of-bounds write.
- CVE-2020-11898 (9.1): length inconsistency in IPv4/ICMPv4, an out-of-bounds read.
- CVE-2020-11901 (9.0): improper input validation in the DNS resolver, possible remote code execution.

CERT/CC's [VU#257161](https://www.kb.cert.org/vuls/id/257161) says most were "caused by memory management bugs".

The supply chain made it hard. CISA notes the stack "may be known by other names such as Kasago TCP/IP, ELMIC, Net+ OS, Quadnet, GHNET v2, Kwiknet, or AMX", and CERT/CC says that because it was licensed as source, modified, or linked statically, "the lack of supply chain visibility has exasperated the problem". The fix was Treck version 6.0.1.67, but each device maker had to ship its own update; CISA's advisory lists separate advisories from medical, industrial and building-automation vendors.

The core bug class, **length parameter inconsistency** (CWE-130), is one you know from the prerequisites: a header field says how long the data is, the code trusts it, and it disagrees with how many bytes actually arrived. The toy below is our own protocol, not Treck's code: two length bytes, then a payload. The vulnerable handler copies `claimed - 2` bytes into a 16-byte buffer. The fixed one checks the claim against the bytes received and the buffer size.

blocks.caption: Compiled with -fsanitize=address. Output: fixed ok: 4 / fixed lie: -1 / vuln ok: 4. With an argument the vulnerable handler is called on the lying packet.

blocks.md:
What AddressSanitizer reports when the vulnerable handler meets the lying packet (claims 64 bytes, sends 6):

```
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow
READ of size 62 at 0x00016f48e2a6 thread T0
    #1 0x00010097102c in handle_vuln lenbug.c:9
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow lenbug.c:9 in handle_vuln
```

The copy starts at byte 2, so it reads 58 bytes beyond the end of the 6-byte packet; the same `memcpy` would also write 62 bytes into a 16-byte buffer. The fix works because both lengths are checked before any copy: the claim must not exceed what arrived (no over-read) and the payload must fit the buffer (no overflow).

blocks.title: A packet that lies about its length

scenes.caption: Six bytes arrived. The first two say the packet is 0x0040 = 64 bytes long. Cells marked ? are memory beyond the packet.
Vulnerable: memcpy copies 62 bytes. After the four real payload bytes it keeps reading whatever lies beyond the packet.
And it writes all 62 into a 16-byte buffer (simplified: only its first 10 cells are drawn), so 46 bytes land past its end on the stack: the start of remote code execution in a real stack.
Fixed: claimed (64) is greater than received (6), so the handler returns -1 before copying anything.

blocks.md: Microcontrollers make such bugs worse. Many have no memory management unit, so no ASLR (address space layout randomisation) and often no non-executable memory unless the maker configures the optional MPU (memory protection unit). The Mirai study's authors urged IoT developers to apply "ASLR, isolation boundaries, and principles of least privilege". Long term, writing parsers in memory-safe languages removes the bug class (the last lesson of *Memory safety bugs*). In the meantime, fuzz every parser (the FDA's guidance asks medical device makers for fuzz testing evidence).

**Defender view.** CERT/CC's note lists network mitigations for devices you cannot patch yet: normalise or reject IP fragments (pieces of one packet split to fit the link) if unused, block IP-in-IP and IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnelling (one packet carried inside another, which several Ripple20 bugs parse), reject malformed TCP, use DHCP snooping, and route DNS through a secure recursive resolver. It also published Suricata (open-source intrusion detection) rules, such as one that alerts on fragments inside an IP-in-IP tunnel:

```
alert ip any any -> any any (msg:"VU#257161:CVE-2020-11896, CVE-2020-11900 Fragments inside IP-in-IP tunnel https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/257161"; ip_proto:4; fragbits:M; sid:1367257161; rev:1;)
```

`ip_proto:4` matches IP-in-IP; `fragbits:M` matches packets with the more-fragments flag. The real fix is still the vendor update, which depends on knowing you ship the stack (lesson 14).

blocks.question: A hospital runs infusion pumps from a vendor that has not yet shipped a Ripple20 fix. Which response matches CERT/CC's guidance?
options: Block IP-in-IP tunnelling and unneeded fragments at the network edge of the pumps' segment, monitor with the published IDS rules, and press the vendor for the update
Wait for the update and change nothing
Disable the pumps' network entirely forever
Replace the hospital's firewall with a newer model
blocks.explain: CERT/CC lists filtering of tunnelling, fragments and malformed traffic plus detection rules as interim measures while the vendor's patch is pending. Doing nothing leaves the risk; permanently disconnecting may stop clinical workflows; a new firewall without the specific rules changes nothing.

blocks.question: In the toy handler, which check prevents the over-read of the received packet?
options: claimed - 2 > sizeof buf
claimed > rx_len
rx_len < 2
claimed < 2
blocks.explain: claimed > rx_len rejects packets whose header promises more bytes than arrived, which is exactly the inconsistency. The buffer-size check stops the overflow of buf; rx_len < 2 and claimed < 2 handle truncated headers and underflow of claimed - 2.

lessons.title: Network exposure: closed by default, segmented, and the Jeep case

blocks.md:
Every listening port on a device is code that strangers can talk to before logging in. The Mirai authors' advice was for IoT to move "away from default-open ports to default-closed". ETSI EN 303 645 provision 5.6-1 says all unused network and logical interfaces "shall be disabled", with the example that an admin interface meant for the LAN "is not accessible from the WAN by default". Provision 5.6-2 adds that a device should not volunteer security-relevant details, such as its software version, to unauthenticated callers, because scanners use that to find vulnerable units.

Tiny example: a camera ships with its web admin page, Telnet and a debug service all listening on every interface. Turning off the two it does not need removes two pre-login attack surfaces from every unit sold.

Exposure also happens without the maker's help. **UPnP** (Universal Plug and Play) lets a device ask the home router to open a port to the internet for it, without the owner seeing. CISA's Mirai alert advised to "Disable Universal Plug and Play (UPnP) on routers unless absolutely necessary." The better design is for devices to make only outbound connections to the maker's cloud and accept commands over that connection, so nothing listens on the internet at all.

**Case: Jeep Cherokee, 2015.** Researchers Charlie Miller and Chris Valasek showed they could reach a Uconnect infotainment unit, made by Harman for Fiat Chrysler (FCA), over the Sprint cellular network. CISA's advisory [ICSA-15-260-01](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-15-260-01) describes the flaw as missing authorization (CVE-2015-5611): the unit "allowed an unauthenticated connection from other access points on the Sprint Network", and from it commands could reach other control units in the vehicle. They had coordinated with FCA for nearly nine months before going public.

The fix came in two layers. NHTSA's (the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration) [recall query summary](https://static.nhtsa.gov/odi/inv/2015/INCLA-RQ15004-9129.PDF) records that FCA and Sprint "conducted a nationwide campaign to block access to a radio communications port that was unintentionally left open", and that FCA launched recall 15V-461 on 23 July 2015 for about 1.4 million vehicles, mailing owners a USB drive with updated software. Network blocking stopped remote exploitation at once; the software update fixed the units themselves.

blocks.title: Uconnect 2015: the open port and the two-layer fix

scenes.caption: Before the fix: a device on the carrier's network could open a connection to the head unit's service. No authentication was required.
From the head unit, messages could reach other control units, which is why NHTSA treated it as a safety recall.
Fix 1, network: the carrier blocked traffic to the port across its network. Exploitation from outside stopped immediately for every vehicle.
Fix 2, device: recall 15V-461 updated the head unit software from a USB stick mailed to owners or at a dealer, not over the carrier network, so the unit itself no longer trusted strangers.

blocks.md: **Segmentation** limits what a compromised device can reach, and what can reach it. You met VLANs and firewalls in the prerequisites. For devices the useful rule is an **egress allowlist**: a camera needs its cloud, its update server and a time server, nothing else. [RFC 8520](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8520.html) (March 2019) defines **MUD** (Manufacturer Usage Description): a file published by the maker, located through a URL the device announces (for example in DHCP), stating what network access the device needs, so the network can enforce it. Its stated aim is to "substantially reduce the threat surface on a device to those communications intended by the manufacturer."

blocks.code:
# Toy egress policy for an IoT VLAN, in the spirit of a MUD file (RFC 8520):
# the maker declares what the camera needs; everything else is dropped.
POLICY = {
    "camera": [("tcp", "api.cam.example", 443),   # cloud upload
               ("tcp", "fw.cam.example", 443),    # signed updates
               ("udp", "ntp.example", 123)],      # time
}

def decide(kind, proto, host, port):
    allowed = (proto, host, port) in POLICY.get(kind, [])
    return "ALLOW" if allowed else "DROP + log"

flows = [("tcp", "api.cam.example", 443),
         ("udp", "ntp.example", 123),
         ("tcp", "203.0.113.50", 23),       # Telnet to a random address
         ("tcp", "198.51.100.7", 2323),     # the other Mirai port
         ("tcp", "nas.home.lan", 445)]      # sideways into the LAN
for f in flows:
    print(f"{f[0]}/{f[2]:<5} {f[1]:<16} -> {decide('camera', *f)}")
blocks.caption: A toy MUD-style policy enforced at the IoT VLAN. Output: the cloud (tcp/443) and time (udp/123) flows print ALLOW; Telnet to 203.0.113.50:23, port 2323 and the LAN file server on 445 print DROP + log.

blocks.md:
The dropped lines are the interesting ones: an infected camera scanning for Telnet (exactly Mirai's behaviour) and a camera trying to reach a file server on the LAN. With an allowlist, both fail and both leave a log line a defender can alert on.

End-of-life devices are the hardest case. The KV botnet that CISA's advisory [AA24-038A](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-038a) links to Volt Typhoon, a state-sponsored hacking group from the People's Republic of China, was built from end-of-life Cisco and NETGEAR small office routers that no longer received updates; the only real fix is replacement, as ETSI 5.3-15A/B anticipates by asking that unupdatable devices be isolable and replaceable.

blocks.question: A smart TV maker wants its app to work when the owner is away. Which design exposes the least attack surface?
options: Ask the home router via UPnP to forward a port to the TV
Tell owners to put the TV in the router's DMZ
Listen on a high, unusual port number
Have the TV hold an outbound, authenticated connection to the maker's cloud and receive commands over it
blocks.explain: An outbound connection means nothing on the TV listens on the internet. UPnP and DMZ (a router setting that forwards all unsolicited inbound traffic to one device) both publish the TV's services to everyone, and an unusual port number is found by scanners anyway.

blocks.question: Within days of the Jeep disclosure, remote exploitation was blocked for all affected vehicles, before most had their software updated. How?
options: Every car downloaded an over-the-air update
NHTSA disabled the vehicles
The cellular carrier blocked traffic to the vulnerable port on its network
Owners turned off their radios
blocks.explain: NHTSA and CISA both record that Sprint blocked access to the port across its network. The software fix followed by USB stick and dealers under recall 15V-461. Network-level blocking is a fast, fleet-wide stopgap when the network path is shared.

lessons.title: The cloud is part of the device: the Verkada case

blocks.md:
Most connected devices are controlled through the maker's cloud: the phone app talks to the cloud, the cloud talks to the device. That makes the cloud, and every employee tool attached to it, part of each device's attack surface. A flaw there reaches every customer at once, with no need to touch a single unit.

Tiny example: support staff need to see a customer's camera to fix a problem. If the support tool can open any camera of any customer, then whoever takes over one support account can too.

**Case: Verkada, 2020 to 2021.** Verkada sells cloud-managed security cameras to businesses. In August 2024 the US Department of Justice filed a complaint on behalf of the FTC (Federal Trade Commission), and the company settled. The complaint (case 3:24-cv-06153, N.D. Cal.) alleges, among other things, two incidents.

What the complaint alleges happened:

- **December 2020**: an intruder used a flaw in a legacy *firmware build server* whose security settings an employee had not restored, installed Mirai and launched denial-of-service attacks from it. Verkada noticed only when AWS (Amazon Web Services) flagged the activity over two weeks later; logging gaps meant nobody could tell whether data was taken.
