- **March 2021**: another intruder exploited a vulnerability in the *customer support server* to gain a support account with "Super Admin" privileges, reaching over 150,000 live customer cameras, including in psychiatric hospitals and clinics. The company learned of it from the media.

These are the government's allegations, taken from the complaint. A Verkada spokesperson [told The Register](https://theregister.com/2024/09/05/verkada_ftc_settlement/) there was "no evidence that the hacker accessed more than a subset of the cameras owned by 97 customers", out of about 6,000. [The Record](https://therecord.media/verkada-security-camera-fined-3-million-ftc) summarises the settlement.

blocks.title: How one support account reached every customer's camera

scenes.caption: Allegation, step 1: an intruder exploits a vulnerability in the support server, which the complaint ties to a scheduled server update done without proper precautions.
Step 2: the server gives access to a support account with Super Admin rights, a single identity trusted across all customers.
Step 3: through the customer platform, that account can open live feeds of over 150,000 cameras. Blast radius: every customer at once.
Missing piece: no centralised alerting noticed hours of unusual access. The company heard about it from a reporter.

blocks.md: The complaint also lists the measures that, in the government's view, would have prevented or limited the breach: training engineers on configuration updates, scanning code repositories for unsecured credentials, least privilege so that few accounts hold privileged access, alerts when files are created, deleted or taken from high-priority servers, and centralised logging and alerting. The order requires a comprehensive information security program with regular independent assessments; the USD 2.95 million civil penalty itself was for violations of the CAN-SPAM Act (a US law on commercial email), not for the breach.

Two device lessons sit inside this case. First, a **firmware build server** is a crown jewel: whoever controls it may control what every device runs, so it deserves the same protection as the signing key (lesson 6). Second, **support access** should be scoped, time-limited and granted by the customer, so that no single staff account can see everyone. A toy version:

blocks.code:
import time
# Support staff reach a customer's cameras only through a grant the
# customer issued: scoped to one site, time-limited, and logged.
grants = {}
audit = []

def customer_grants(site, engineer, minutes):
    grants[(site, engineer)] = time.time() + minutes * 60

def view_camera(engineer, site, cam, now=None):
    now = now or time.time()
    exp = grants.get((site, engineer))
    ok = exp is not None and now < exp
    audit.append((engineer, site, cam, "ok" if ok else "denied"))
    return "stream" if ok else "DENIED"

customer_grants("clinic-12", "eng-ana", minutes=30)
print(view_camera("eng-ana", "clinic-12", "cam-3"))
print(view_camera("eng-ana", "school-4", "cam-1"))        # no grant there
print(view_camera("eng-ana", "clinic-12", "cam-3", now=time.time() + 3600))
print(audit)
blocks.caption: Output: stream / DENIED / DENIED, then the audit list with one ok and two denied entries. The third call is an hour later, after the 30-minute grant expired.

blocks.md:
**Defender view.**
- *Prevent*: MFA (multi-factor authentication) and least privilege for every staff tool; customer-approved, expiring support grants; build and signing systems on their own hardened network; secret scanning in repositories.
- *Detect*: centralised logs for the support platform with alerts on one account opening many customers' devices, unusual hours, and bulk downloads. Treat outbound attack traffic from your own servers (as in December 2020) as a sign of compromise, not just of abuse.
- *Respond*: revoke sessions and tokens, rotate credentials the server held, and rebuild compromised servers from scratch, which is what the forensic firm in the complaint recommended for the build server.

blocks.question: Which change most reduces the blast radius of a stolen support account in a camera cloud?
options: Support access that requires a time-limited grant from each customer and covers only that customer's devices
Longer passwords for support staff
Encrypting video at rest
Moving the support server to a different cloud provider
blocks.explain: Blast radius is how much one compromised identity can reach. Per-customer, expiring grants mean a stolen account sees only what is currently granted. Longer passwords make theft harder but do not limit reach; encryption at rest does not stop a privileged user viewing live feeds.

blocks.question: Why does the complaint's December 2020 incident, a botnet on a build server, matter for device security even if no camera was touched?
options: Build servers have no security relevance
Mirai can infect cameras through the cloud
Whoever controls the build path may be able to put code into the firmware that every device runs
Because AWS charges for outbound traffic
blocks.explain: A build server sits on the path from source to signed firmware. An intruder there could alter what is built, which secure boot would then accept if it gets signed. That is why build and signing systems are part of the supply chain position in the threat model.

lessons.title: Device vulnerability handling: disclosure, SBOMs and the CRA

blocks.md:
Devices will ship with bugs. What separates a responsible maker is what happens next: can a researcher report a bug, can the maker find which products contain an affected component, can it ship a fix, and for how long will it keep doing so? This lesson covers the machinery for each, and the EU law that now makes it mandatory.

Tiny example: on the day Ripple20 was published, a maker of infusion pumps had to answer one question fast: do any of our products contain the Treck stack, and which versions? Without a component list, that takes weeks of digging through vendors' code.

**Receiving reports.** ETSI EN 303 645 provision 5.2-1 requires a public vulnerability disclosure policy, and UK PSTI requires a contact plus the timescales for acknowledgement and status updates (lesson 4). A simple way to publish the contact is `security.txt`, defined in [RFC 9116](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9116.html) (April 2022): a text file at `/.well-known/security.txt` on your website. Two fields are required: `Contact` (how to report, "MUST always be present") and `Expires` (when the file becomes stale; RFC 9116 recommends less than a year ahead).

blocks.code:
# https://cam.example/.well-known/security.txt
Contact: mailto:security@cam.example
Contact: https://cam.example/security/report
Expires: 2027-10-31T23:59:00z
Encryption: https://cam.example/security/pgp-key.txt
Policy: https://cam.example/security/disclosure-policy
Preferred-Languages: en, de
blocks.caption: A security.txt for the doorbell camera's maker. The policy page should state the acknowledgement and update timescales PSTI asks for.

blocks.md: **Knowing what you ship.** An **SBOM** (software bill of materials) is a machine-readable list of the components inside a product, like the ingredients list on food. The US NTIA's (National Telecommunications and Information Administration, part of the Department of Commerce) 2021 [minimum elements report](https://www.ntia.gov/sites/default/files/publications/sbom_minimum_elements_report_0.pdf) lists the fields every entry needs (CISA published an updated draft of these minimum elements for comment in 2025): supplier name, component name, version, other unique identifiers, dependency relationship, author of the SBOM data, and a timestamp. CycloneDX, an OWASP standard (now also [Ecma standard ECMA-424](https://cyclonedx.org/specification/overview/)), is a common format. The FDA requires an SBOM for medical "cyber devices" (lesson 15). General SBOM practice is covered in *Software supply chain security*; for firmware, two problems stand out: vendor libraries delivered as binaries without versions, and the same code under different names, as Ripple20's aliases showed.

blocks.code:
{"bomFormat": "CycloneDX", "specVersion": "1.6",
 "metadata": {"component": {"type": "firmware", "name": "infusion-hub-fw", "version": "3.2.0"}},
 "components": [
  {"type": "library", "supplier": {"name": "Treck Inc."}, "name": "Treck TCP/IP", "version": "6.0.1.28"},
  {"type": "library", "name": "mbedtls", "version": "3.6.2"},
  {"type": "library", "name": "vendor-radio-blob"}]}
blocks.caption: A toy firmware SBOM. The third entry has no version: a typical gap in binary-only vendor code.

Matching the SBOM against the Ripple20 advisory. Output: firmware: infusion-hub-fw 3.2.0 / AFFECTED Treck TCP/IP 6.0.1.28 (fixed in 6.0.1.67) / ok mbedtls 3.6.2 / UNKNOWN vendor-radio-blob: no version, ask the supplier

blocks.md:
**The EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA)** applies to "products with digital elements" sold in the EU, connected devices included. Per the [Commission's summary](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-summary), it entered into force on 10 December 2024 and is fully applicable from 11 December 2027. Manufacturers must meet the essential requirements of Annex I, which has a part on product security and a part on vulnerability handling, perform a cybersecurity risk assessment, and set a **support period** whose end date (month and year) is stated at the time of purchase.

The reporting duty started earlier, on **11 September 2026**, and covers products already on the market. When a manufacturer becomes aware of an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe incident, it notifies its national CSIRT (computer security incident response team) and ENISA (the EU Agency for Cybersecurity) through ENISA's single reporting platform.

blocks.title: CRA clocks after learning of an exploited vulnerability

scenes.caption: Day 0: the manufacturer becomes aware that a vulnerability in its product is being actively exploited.
Within 24 hours: an early warning notification, through ENISA's single reporting platform to the national CSIRT.
Within 72 hours: the main notification with more detail.
The manufacturer ships a fix (here on day 7). A final report is due no later than 14 days after a corrective or mitigating measure is available.

blocks.md: Coordinated disclosure for embedded bugs usually takes longer than for web software, because every downstream maker must build, test and ship. Ripple20 is the pattern: researchers reported to CERT/CC, which coordinated with Treck and downstream vendors before publication, and CISA kept updating its advisory for months as vendors published their own (updates A to G in 2020 alone). ETSI 5.2-3 asks manufacturers to keep monitoring for and fixing vulnerabilities in the products they sell, and lesson 9's update machinery is what lets them deliver the fixes.

Vulnerability handling is a pipeline: a published way to receive reports, an SBOM to find affected products, a signed update path to fix them, a stated support period, and (in the EU) 24-hour, 72-hour and final reports for exploited bugs. Missing any stage breaks the rest.

blocks.question: A maker's SBOM lists 'vendor-radio-blob' with no version. A new advisory affects some versions of a radio driver. What is the right next step?
options: Assume it is not affected because the SBOM shows no matching version
Treat it as unknown: ask the supplier for the exact component and version, and track it as a possible exposure until answered
Delete the entry from the SBOM
Mark the product as affected and recall it at once
blocks.explain: An entry without a version cannot be matched, so the honest status is unknown. The fix is to get the data from the supplier (and require it in contracts). Assuming 'not affected' hides risk; deleting the entry loses information; an immediate recall is premature.

blocks.question: Under the CRA, which deadline applies to a manufacturer's first notification of an actively exploited vulnerability?
options: 24 hours for an early warning
72 hours
14 days
One month
blocks.explain: The early warning is due within 24 hours, the main notification within 72 hours, and the final report no later than 14 days after a fix or mitigation is available. One month is the final-report deadline for severe incidents.

lessons.title: Medical devices: FDA section 524B, pacemakers and insulin pumps

blocks.md:
In a medical device, a security bug can become a safety problem: a wrong dose, a stopped heartbeat, a drained battery in an implant. And the usual remedies are harder: an implant cannot be swapped like a router, and an update itself carries clinical risk.

Tiny example: an insulin pump accepts radio commands from a remote control. If the pump checks only that a command is well formed, anyone nearby who records "deliver 2 units" can play it back, or change the number.

**Case: Medtronic MiniMed pumps (2019).** CISA's advisory [ICSMA-19-178-01](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-medical-advisories/icsma-19-178-01) (CVE-2019-10964, CVSS 7.1) states that the radio protocol between certain MiniMed insulin pumps and their accessories "does not properly implement authentication or authorization", so an attacker with adjacent access "can inject, replay, modify, and/or intercept data" and could "change pump settings and control insulin delivery". The FDA said Medtronic was unable to adequately update the affected models with any software or patch. Medtronic advised US patients to talk to their doctors about switching to newer pumps, and listed precautions: keep the pump physically controlled, do not share its serial number, watch alerts and cancel unintended boluses (a bolus is a single dose given all at once).

blocks.title: Replay against a toy pump, and the fix

scenes.caption: The patient's remote sends 'bolus 2.0u'. The attacker's radio records the frame.
Vulnerable pump: the replayed frame is well formed, so the pump delivers a second, unintended dose.

Fixed pump: each frame carries a counter and a MAC (message authentication code, a keyed checksum; not the MAC address of lesson 3) under a key set at pairing. The original frame, counter 41, is accepted.
The replay repeats counter 41, which is not newer than the last accepted one: rejected. A modified dose breaks the MAC: rejected.

blocks.code:
import hmac, hashlib

# Vulnerable toy pump: acts on any well-formed radio frame
def pump_v1(frame):
    return "DELIVER " + frame.decode()

# Fixed toy pump: frames carry a counter and a MAC under a paired key
KEY = bytes.fromhex("8f" * 16)          # set during pairing, per device
last_seen = 0
def make_frame(counter, cmd):
    body = counter.to_bytes(4, "big") + cmd
    return body + hmac.new(KEY, body, hashlib.sha256).digest()[:8]

def pump_v2(frame):
    global last_seen
    body, tag = frame[:-8], frame[-8:]
    good = hmac.new(KEY, body, hashlib.sha256).digest()[:8]
    if not hmac.compare_digest(tag, good):
        return "REJECT: bad MAC"
    counter = int.from_bytes(body[:4], "big")
    if counter <= last_seen:
        return "REJECT: replay"
    last_seen = counter
    return "DELIVER " + body[4:].decode()

sniffed = b"bolus 2.0u"
print("v1 original:", pump_v1(sniffed))
print("v1 replay  :", pump_v1(sniffed))             # recorded and resent
f = make_frame(41, b"bolus 2.0u")
print("v2 original:", pump_v2(f))
print("v2 replay  :", pump_v2(f))
forged = f[:4] + b"bolus 9.0u" + f[-8:]
print("v2 modified:", pump_v2(forged))
blocks.caption: Toy model of the fix. Output: v1 original: DELIVER bolus 2.0u / v1 replay  : DELIVER bolus 2.0u / v2 original: DELIVER bolus 2.0u / v2 replay  : REJECT: replay / v2 modified: REJECT: bad MAC

blocks.md: Why the fix works: the MAC (message authentication code: a checksum computed with a secret key, here HMAC-SHA-256, the standard keyed-hash MAC built on SHA-256, so only a key holder can produce a valid one) proves the frame came from a paired device and was not altered, and the counter proves it is new. Both are needed: a MAC alone happily verifies a replayed frame. The FDA's guidance recommends exactly this, "anti-replay measures in critical communications such as potentially harmful commands", using for example cryptographic nonces (random values used only once, so a recorded message cannot be accepted twice).

**Case: Abbott (St. Jude Medical) pacemakers (2017).** CISA's advisory [ICSMA-17-241-01](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-medical-advisories/icsma-17-241-01), based on findings by the firm MedSec, lists three issues in radio-enabled pacemakers: an authentication algorithm that "can be compromised or bypassed" by a nearby attacker (CVE-2017-12712), no limit on "RF wake-up" commands so an attacker could drain the battery (CVE-2017-12714), and unencrypted patient data (CVE-2017-12716). Abbott's firmware update, applied in a clinic with a programmer, added wake-up protections and limited the commands accepted over radio; pacemakers built from 28 August 2017 shipped with it. Because updating carried its own risk, the advisory left the decision to each patient and physician, and suggested pacing-dependent patients be updated where temporary pacing was available.

The FDA's premarket guidance, *[Cybersecurity in Medical Devices: Quality Management System Considerations and Content of Premarket Submissions](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/cybersecurity-medical-devices-quality-system-considerations-and-content-premarket-submissions)* (February 2026, superseding the June 2025 version), sets security objectives (authenticity including integrity, authorization, availability, confidentiality, and secure and timely updatability) and asks for a threat model, security architecture views, an SBOM in machine-readable form with each component's support status, and testing evidence including fuzz testing and checks for hard-coded, default or easily guessed credentials. It is the most complete public checklist for any device, medical or not.

A medical maker cannot ship fixes as casually as a phone maker: each change may need risk review, and an implant update happens in a clinic. That is why FDA expects the update path and the postmarket plan to be designed before approval, not invented after a disclosure.

blocks.question: A toy pump adds a MAC to each command frame but no counter or nonce. Which attack still works?
options: Changing the dose in a recorded frame
Sending a command without the key
None
Replaying a recorded frame unchanged
blocks.explain: A MAC detects changes and forgery, so altering the dose or sending without the key both fail. But a recorded frame is unchanged, so its MAC still verifies: without a counter, nonce or timestamp the pump cannot tell new from old. That is why the FDA lists anti-replay separately.

blocks.question: A wearable heart monitor syncs to a phone only over Bluetooth and never directly to the internet. Under FDA's reading of section 524B, could it be a cyber device?
options: No, it has no internet connection
Yes: FDA treats Bluetooth and other radio links as an ability to connect to the internet
Only if it stores data in the cloud
Only if it has a USB port
blocks.explain: The FDA FAQ lists Bluetooth and BLE among the features it considers to give the ability to connect to the internet, since the phone relays the data. So the device can meet the definition, along with having software and characteristics that could be vulnerable.

lessons.title: A secure device end to end, and where to practise

blocks.md:
You now have every piece. This last lesson puts them in the order a product team meets them, from chip choice to end of life, and points you to legal places to practise.

Tiny example: the doorbell camera, designed again with this course in hand. Each line below names the lesson that justifies it.

blocks.title: The doorbell camera, secured from factory to retirement

nodes.label:
Chip: secure boot,
OTP, glitch detect

Factory: unique keys,
passwords, debug locked

End of support:
published date, isolate

scenes.caption: Choose a chip with secure boot, OTP for keys and locks, debug lockdown and fault countermeasures (lessons 1, 5 to 7).
At the factory: per-device keys born in a secure element, a random label password or forced setup, debug and download modes locked, fuse state logged (lessons 3, 5, 8).
In the home: nothing unneeded listening, every parser bounds-checked and fuzzed, outbound-only to the cloud behind an allowlist (lessons 11, 12).
In the cloud: scoped, logged support access with MFA (lesson 13).
Over its life: reports come in, the SBOM finds affected units, signed A/B updates fix them, and the published support date tells owners when to replace it (lessons 9, 10, 14).

blocks.md: A compact cross-check is NIST IR 8259A ([May 2020](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2020/NIST.IR.8259A.pdf)), the US National Institute of Standards and Technology's core baseline of device capabilities: device identification, device configuration, data protection, logical access to interfaces, software update and cybersecurity state awareness. Each maps onto lessons here: identity (8), configuration and access (3, 5, 12), data protection (8), update (9, 10), and state awareness, meaning the device can report its own security state (6, 13).

# release-review.yaml: questions to answer before shipping a device
passwords:   unique per unit or set at setup? rate limited?        # L3, L4
debug:       UART prompt off? JTAG/SWD locked in OTP? download off? # L5
boot:        ROM verifies bootloader and app? key fingerprint set?  # L6
physical:    unused boot paths off? glitch detector on?            # L7
secrets:     any secret shared across units? per-device identity?  # L8
updates:     signed manifest? anti-rollback floor? trial boot?     # L9, L10
parsers:     every length checked? fuzzed? stack version known?    # L11
network:     ports closed by default? outbound only? MUD/allowlist? # L12
cloud:       support access scoped and logged? MFA?                # L13

blocks.caption: A one-page release review. Each 'no' is a design decision to make explicitly, not a box to tick later.

blocks.md:
**The legal line.** Test only devices you own or have written permission to test. Buying a device makes it yours to examine, but its maker's cloud and other people's units are not; probing those needs authorisation. Report what you find through the maker's published channel, or through CERT/CC if there is none.

**Where to practise**, all on targets built for learning:
- [OWASP IoTGoat](https://github.com/OWASP/IoTGoat/releases): "a deliberately insecure firmware" based on OpenWrt, to run in an emulator and audit.
- The [OWASP IoT Top 10 (2018)](https://wiki.owasp.org/images/1/1c/OWASP-IoT-Top-10-2018-final.pdf), a one-page list of the most common device weaknesses, to check your own designs against.
- [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/), Carnegie Mellon's free practice platform, for the general skills underneath.
- Your own development board (an ESP32 or RP2350 board costs little): enable secure boot and flash encryption on it, and confirm each lock with the vendor's tools.

Secure devices come from a few decisions made early and kept: nothing shared across units, nothing runs unless signed, nothing listens unless needed, every unit can be updated and the update cannot go backwards, and someone is responsible for bugs until a published end date.

blocks.question: Which single design choice most limits the damage when one unit is fully reverse engineered in a lab?
options: Obfuscating the firmware
Removing the labels from the debug pads
Making sure every key and password on the unit is unique to it, with no fleet-wide secrets
Using a less common chip
blocks.explain: With per-unit secrets, a fully compromised unit gives the attacker only that unit. Obfuscation, hidden pads and unusual chips slow analysis but do not change what is gained once it succeeds.

blocks.question: A device's support period ends next month and the maker will publish no more updates. What does ETSI EN 303 645 suggest for devices that cannot be updated?
options: That they be isolable and their hardware replaceable, with the replacement plan communicated
Nothing: support simply ends
That owners disable the firewall
That the maker publish the signing key
blocks.explain: Provisions 5.3-14 and 5.3-15A/B ask makers to publish the rationale and replacement support, and say such devices should be isolable and replaceable. Publishing the signing key would let anyone push firmware; disabling firewalls increases exposure.
